defects.description: The handler does its own sniffing and calls image.Decode directly instead of using media.Decode. media.Decode already sniffs the content type from the bytes and checks dimensions with DecodeConfig before decoding.

There is no pixel-dimension check before full decode. A small PNG can declare an enormous canvas (decompression bomb) and exhaust pod memory. R3/AC4 (reject over 40 MP without decoding the pixel data) is not implemented.
defects.location: plan.md step 5; spec.md R3, AC4, non-functional constraints

defects.description: The route skips LimitBody, and the handler io.ReadAll's the body (or lets ParseMultipartForm spool it) before checking size. A client can stream an arbitrarily large body into memory or onto disk, which breaks AC2 and the bounded-memory constraint (512 MB pods, about 40 concurrent requests).
defects.location: plan.md steps 1-3, rollout notes; fixture/internal/api/middleware.go LimitBody; fixture/internal/api/server.go

defects.description: The 5 MB limit is applied to the whole request body (ContentLength or bytes read) in both modes. In multipart mode the boundary and part headers push an exactly-5 MB image over the limit, so AC1 ('exactly 5,242,880 bytes accepted ... as a multipart upload') fails. R1 sets the limit on the image itself.

The previous version's objects are deleted before the new version is committed with SetAvatarVersion. If the update fails or conflicts, the user is left pointing at deleted objects, which breaks AC5. A racing upload's conflict path also removes the winner's predecessor.
R6/AC6 (GET /v1/me includes the avatar object, or null) is not in the plan. meResponse in profile.go is never extended.

There are no tests for AC2 (oversize gives 413 with bounded memory), AC4 (48 MP gives 422), AC5 (DB failure keeps the old avatar working) or the exactly-5 MB multipart boundary in AC1. The plan also says no media tests are needed, although it relies on new dimension behaviour.

tensions.description: Architecture's natural fix is to call media.Decode, which already sniffs the type and checks dimensions before decoding. But media.Decode's MaxPixels is a package constant of 100 MP, sized for catalog product photos, so a plain reuse accepts the 48 MP image AC4 says must be rejected. Risk's natural fix is a 40 MP DecodeConfig check in the handler, which duplicates the logic architecture wants centralised. The conflict only shows up once you read the constant in imageproc.go.
tensions.lens_a_fix: Replace the handler's sniffing and image.Decode with media.Decode.
tensions.lens_b_fix: Run image.DecodeConfig in the avatar handler and reject anything over 40 MP before decoding.
tensions.reconciliation: Reuse media.Decode but make the pixel limit a parameter or option (for example DecodeWithLimit(r, maxPixels), with the existing Decode keeping 100 MP for catalog callers). The avatar handler passes 40 MP and maps ErrTooLarge to 422 image_too_large. Add a media test for the limit.

tensions.description: Risk's natural fix is to put the route behind LimitBody(5 << 20) so the body can never exceed 5 MB. Consistency notes that the limit is on the image, not the request: with a strict 5 MB body cap, an exactly-5 MB image uploaded as multipart is rejected, which breaks AC1. Consistency's fix (allow the full image plus multipart overhead) looks like loosening the limit risk just tightened. The disagreement is over the exact limit value and where it is applied.
tensions.lens_a_fix: Wrap the route in LimitBody(5 << 20) and stop using io.ReadAll and ParseMultipartForm on unbounded input.
tensions.lens_b_fix: Apply the 5 MB limit to the image bytes (the raw body or the file part), not to the whole multipart request.
tensions.reconciliation: Apply LimitBody at 5 MB plus a small fixed multipart allowance (for example 64 KB). Stream multipart with r.MultipartReader() instead of ParseMultipartForm, and read the file part through an io.LimitReader of 5 MB + 1 byte, returning 413 if it overflows. Raw bodies get exactly 5 MB. Memory stays bounded and AC1/AC2 both hold.
